Mutual-visibility coloring of graphs

Saneesh Babu Note: saneeshbabu1996@gmail.com Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Cochin University of Science and TechnologyCochin - 22, Kerala, India    Gabriele Di Stefano Note: gabriele.distefano@univaq.it Affiliation: Department of Information Engineering, Computer Science and MathematicsUniversity of L’Aquila, Italy    Aparna Lakshmanan S Note: aparnaren@gmail.com, aparnals@cusat.ac.in Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Cochin University of Science and TechnologyCochin - 22, Kerala, India
Abstract

The mutual-visibility chromatic number of a graph GG is the smallest number of colors needed to color the vertices of GG such that each color class is a mutual-visibility set. In this paper, we prove that determining the mutual-visibility chromatic number of a graph is NP-complete even when restricted to the class of graphs having diameter four and mutual-visibility chromatic number two. We further determine the exact value of the mutual-visibility chromatic number for glued binary trees and glued tt-ary trees.

Keywords: Mutual-visibility number, mutual-visibility chromatic number, computational complexity, glued binary tree, glued tt-ary tree

AMS Subj. Class. (2020): 05C15, 68Q17, 05C69

1 Introduction

The no-three-in-line problem is a classical problem in discrete geometry known from games in various cultures since ancient times [13, 24]. It has been a subject of mathematical study in combinatorics after Dudeney’s chessboard puzzle which was proposed in the early twentieth century [10]. This problem was later generalized to larger grids and planes [12, 18, 19, 20]. Graph theoretic version of this problem was introduced independently in 20162016 and 20182018 under the names geodesic irredundant sets [6] and general position sets [17], respectively. Later, the graph theoretic version of the problem is popular under the name general position problem which has been recently surveyed in [5], see also [1, 15, 16, 21]. Subsequently, several variations of this problem emerged [22], among which the most extensively studied is the mutual-visibility variant, first introduced by Di Stefano in 20222022 [9]. A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is mutually visible if for every x,y∈Sx,y\in S, there exists a shortest x−yx-y path with no internal vertices in SS. Beyond its application in computer science, particularly in robot visibility, the mutual-visibility problem connects to combinatorial problems such as Zarankiewicz and Turan problems [7, 8, 11].

In 20242024, Sandi Klavžar et al. introduced a vertex coloring of graphs in which each color class is a mutual-visibility set [14]. The mutual-visibility coloring is defined as follows: two vertices x,y∈V⁡(G)x,y\in V(G) can be given the same color if there exists an x−yx-y geodesic path whose internal vertices have colors different from that of xx and yy. The smallest number of colors required for such a coloring of GG is called mutual-visibility chromatic number, denoted by χμ​(G)\chi_{\mu}(G). Following this, vertex coloring based on general position sets [4], independent mutual-visibility sets [3] and distance mutual-visibility sets [2] have also been investigated.

It is proved in [4] that the general position problem is NP-complete even when restricted to the class of graphs with diameter two and general position number three. The concept of independent general position coloring is also introduced and proved to be NP-complete even when restricted to the class of graphs with diameter at most three. In [14], computing the computational complexity of mutual-visibility chromatic number is left as an interesting problem for further investigation. The decision problem arising from the independent version of mutual-visibility coloring [3] is proved to be NP-complete even in graphs with universal vertices and the authors conjectured that mutual-visibility coloring is NP-complete.

A perfect tt-ary tree, Tr,tT_{r,t} of depth r≥1r\geq 1, is a rooted tree in which all non-leaf vertices have tt children, and all leaves have depth rr. It has tr+1−1t−1\frac{t^{r+1}-1}{t-1} vertices and trt^{r} leaves. For t≥2t\geq 2 and r≥1r\geq 1, a glued tt-ary tree, G​T​(r,t)GT(r,t) is obtained from two copies of Tr,tT_{r,t} by pairwise identifying their leaves [15]. The vertices obtained by identification are called quasi-leaves of G​T​(r,t)GT(r,t) and the set of quasi-leaves of G​T​(r,t)GT(r,t) will be denoted by L⁡(G​T​(r,t))L(GT(r,t)). For a vertex uu in G​T​(r,t)GT(r,t), TuT_{u} denotes the tree rooted in uu and having as leaves all the descendants of uu that are quasi-leaves.

The perfect 22-ary and glued 22-ary trees are called perfect binary trees and glued binary trees [17], respectively. We will simplify the notation by setting G​T​(r)=G​T​(r,2)GT(r)=GT(r,2). We will denote the two copies of Tr,2T_{r,2}, from which G​T​(r)GT(r) is constructed, by Tr(1)T_{r}^{(1)} and Tr(2)T_{r}^{(2)}, so that L⁡(G​T​(r))=V⁡(Tr(1))∩V⁡(Tr(2))L(GT(r))=V(T_{r}^{(1)})\cap V(T_{r}^{(2)}). Moreover, we set Vr(1)=V⁡(T1(1))\L⁡(G​T​(r))V_{r}^{(1)}=V(T_{1}^{(1)})\backslash L(GT(r)) and Vr(2)=V⁡(T1(2))\L⁡(G​T​(r))V_{r}^{(2)}=V(T_{1}^{(2)})\backslash L(GT(r)).

In this paper, the mutual-visibility coloring problem is proved to be NP-complete settling the conjecture. In view of its computational complexity, it is natural to study this parameter in specific graph classes. In the last section we determine the exact values of mutual-visibility coloring for glued binary trees and extend it further the glued tt-ary trees.

2 Computational complexity

To study the computational complexity of finding a mutual-visibility coloring of a graph that uses the smallest possible number of colors, we introduce the following decision problem.

Definition 2.1.

MV-coloring problem:
Instance: A graph GG, a positive integer k≤|V⁡(G)|k\leq|V(G)|.
Question: Is there a mutual-visibility coloring of GG such that χμ​(G)≤k\chi_{\mu}(G)\leq k?

The problem is hard to solve as shown by the next Theorem 2.3. Before proving the theorem, we introduce a graph whose properties are widely used in the proof of the theorem. Let HnH_{n}, n≥2n\geq 2, be the graph consisting of two stars on n+2n+2 vertices where nn leaves are identified. Let cc and pp denote the center and the non-identified leaf of the first star. Let c′c^{\prime} and p′p^{\prime} denote the corresponding vertices of the second star. Let p1,p2,…,pnp_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n} be the identified leaves. A representation of HnH_{n} is given in Figure 1.

Lemma 2.2.

In a mutual-visibility coloring of HnH_{n} with two colors, vertices cc and pp (c′c^{\prime} and p′p^{\prime}, respectively) cannot be colored with the same color. In the set of vertices {p1,p2,…,pn}\{p_{1},p_{2},\ldots,p_{n}\}, at least two vertices are colored with different colors.

Proof.

Consider a mutual-visibility coloring of HnH_{n} using two colors, say red and white. If a pendant vertex and its support vertex are given the same color, then that color cannot be used anywhere else in the graph. Therefore, if pp and cc (equivalently, p′p^{\prime} and c′c^{\prime}) are given the same color, then we require at least three colors to color HnH_{n}. Suppose vertices pp and cc are colored red. Therefore, pp and cc (equivalently, p′p^{\prime} and c′c^{\prime}) must be of different colors. Without loss of generality assume that pp is white and cc is red. Since at least one among c′c^{\prime} and p′p^{\prime} is white (equivalently, red), at least one among {p1,p2,…,pn}\{p_{1},p_{2},...,p_{n}\} must be red (equivalently, white) for mutual-visibility. Hence, the lemma. ∎

Theorem 2.3.

MV-coloring is NP-complete even for instances (G,k)(G,k) with diam(G)=4\mathop{\mathrm{diam}}(G)=4 and k=2k=2.

Proof.

Given a coloring of GG, it is possible to test in polynomial time whether it is a mutual-visibility coloring or not. Consequently, the problem is in NP.

We prove that the NAE3-SAT problem, defined below and shown to be NP-complete in [23], polynomially reduces to MV-coloring.

A NAE3-SAT (not-all-equal 3-satisfiability) instance Φ\Phi is defined as a set X={x1,x2,…,xq}X=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{q}\} of qq Boolean variables and a set CC of rr clauses, each defined as a set of three literals: every variable xix_{i} corresponds to two literals, that is, xix_{i} (the positive form) and x¯i\bar{x}_{i} (the negative form). To simplify the notations we will denote by {ℓ1,ℓ2,ℓ3}\{\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{3}\} the clause with literals ℓi,i∈[3]\ell_{i},i\in[3], without distinction between the orders in which they are listed. A truth assignment assigns a Boolean value (T​r​u​eTrue or F​a​l​s​eFalse) to each variable, corresponding to a truth assignment of opposite values for the two literals xix_{i} and xi¯\bar{x_{i}}: xi¯\bar{x_{i}} is T​r​u​eTrue if and only if xix_{i} is F​a​l​s​eFalse.

The NAE3-SAT problem asks whether there is a truth assignment to the variables such that in no clause all three literals have the same truth value. We will say that such an assignment is satisfying and the instance Φ\Phi is satisfied.

In what follows we assume that in any instance of NAE3-SAT each clause involves three different variables. Indeed, if a clause involves a single variable and all the literals are equal, then the NAE3-SAT problem has a No answer and if the positive and negative form of a variable are present in a clause we can remove the clause from the instance. If a clause involves only two variables, and the variable appearing two times in the clauses is present in the same form, e.g. {l1,l1,l2}\{l_{1},l_{1},l_{2}\}, then the clause is logically equivalent to {l1,l2}\{l_{1},l_{2}\} and it can be substituted with two clauses {l1,l2,a}\{l_{1},l_{2},a\} and {l1,l2,a¯}\{l_{1},l_{2},\bar{a}\}, where aa is an additional variable.

We reduce any instance of NAE3-SAT to an instance of MV-Coloring. Let Φ=(X,C)\Phi=(X,C), with X={x1,x2,…,xq}X=\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{q}\} and C={c1,c2,…,cr}C=\{c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{r}\}, be any instance of NAE3-SAT. We construct a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) in such a way that GG has a mutual-visibility coloring with at most k=2k=2 colors if and only if Φ\Phi admits a satisfying truth assignment.

For each variable xi∈Xx_{i}\in X, i∈[q]i\in[q], there is a true-setting subgraph H2(i)=(Vi,Ei)H_{2}^{(i)}=(V_{i},E_{i}) of GG with Vi={ui,ui¯,ai,bi,p,c}V_{i}=\{u_{i},\bar{u_{i}},a_{i},b_{i},p,c\} and Ei={ui​ai,ui¯​ai,ui​c,ui¯​c,ai​bi,p​c}E_{i}=\{u_{i}a_{i},\bar{u_{i}}a_{i},u_{i}c,\bar{u_{i}}c,a_{i}b_{i},pc\}. Then, each subgraph H2(i)H_{2}^{(i)} is isomorphic to a H2H_{2} graph. Notice that, by Lemma 2.2, the vertices uiu_{i} and ui¯\bar{u_{i}} of H2(i)H_{2}^{(i)} cannot be colored with the same color, as well as the pairs of vertices ai,bia_{i},b_{i} and p,cp,c.

For each clause cj∈Cc_{j}\in C, j∈[r]j\in[r], there is subgraph H3(j)=(Vj,Ej)H_{3}^{(j)}=(V_{j},E_{j}) of GG isomorphic to a H3H_{3} graph where VjV_{j} contains the vertices vj,wj,p,cv_{j},w_{j},p,c and three more vertices depending on cjc_{j}. Let TjT_{j} be the set of these three vertices. If the clause cj={ℓi1,ℓi2,ℓi3}c_{j}=\{\ell_{i_{1}},\ell_{i_{2}},\ell_{i_{3}}\} contains the variables xi1,xi2x_{i_{1}},x_{i_{2}}, and xi3x_{i_{3}} then the three vertices of H3(j)H_{3}^{(j)} in TjT_{j} belong to H2(i1)H_{2}^{(i_{1})}, H2(i2)H_{2}^{(i_{2})}, and H2(i3)H_{2}^{(i_{3})}. In particular if ℓi1=xi1\ell_{i_{1}}=x_{i_{1}} (ℓi1=x¯i1\ell_{i_{1}}=\bar{x}_{i_{1}}, resp.) then ui1u_{i_{1}} (u¯i1\bar{u}_{i_{1}}, resp.) is a vertex of TjT_{j}. Similarly for the vertices corresponding to literals ℓi2\ell_{i_{2}} and ℓi3\ell_{i_{3}}. Set EjE_{j} contains edges p​cpc and vj​wjv_{j}w_{j} and all the edges connecting vertices in {c,vj}\{c,v_{j}\} to vertices in TjT_{j}. Notice that, by Lemma 2.2, vertices in TjT_{j} cannot be colored with the same color. The same happens for the pairs of vertices vjv_{j} and wjw_{j}, j∈[r]j\in[r].

There are two more non-adjacent vertices in VV, that is zz and z′z^{\prime}. These two vertices are adjacent to all the other vertices in the set {ui,ui¯,ai,vj|i∈[q],j∈[r]}\{u_{i},\bar{u_{i}},a_{i},v_{j}~|~i\in[q],j\in[r]\}. Then

V=⋃i∈[q]Vi∪⋃j∈[r]Vj∪{z,z′}V=\bigcup_{i\in[q]}V_{i}\cup\bigcup_{j\in[r]}V_{j}\cup\{z,z^{\prime}\}
E=⋃i∈[q]Ei∪⋃j∈[r]Ej∪{uiζ,u¯iζ,aiζ,viζ|i∈[q],j∈[r],ζ∈{z,z′}}E=\bigcup_{i\in[q]}E_{i}\cup\bigcup_{j\in[r]}E_{j}\cup\left\{u_{i}\zeta,\bar{u}_{i}\zeta,a_{i}\zeta,v_{i}\zeta~|~i\in[q],j\in[r],\zeta\in\{z,z^{\prime}\}\right\}

A representation of the graph GG is given in Figure 2.

It is easy to see that the construction of GG can be accomplished in polynomial time and that diam(G)=4\mathop{\mathrm{diam}}(G)=4. All that remains to be proved is that Φ\Phi is satisfied if and only if GG has a mutual-visibility coloring of size at most two.

(⇒)(\Rightarrow) First, suppose that t:X→{T​r​u​e,F​a​l​s​e}t:X\rightarrow\{True,False\} is a satisfying truth assignment for CC. Then we color the vertices in GG with two colors, namely red, and white, depending on tt. We color the vertices of the following pairs with different colors: p,cp,c; z,z′z,z^{\prime}; ai,bia_{i},b_{i}, for each i∈[q]i\in[q]; vj,wjv_{j},w_{j}, for each j∈[r]j\in[r]. If t⁡(xi)t(x_{i}) is T​r​u​eTrue for a given i∈[p]i\in[p], then the vertex uiu_{i} in subgraph H2(i)H_{2}^{(i)} is colored red and vertex ui¯\bar{u_{i}} is colored white. Conversely, if t⁡(xi)t(x_{i}) is F​a​l​s​eFalse then vertex uiu_{i} is colored white and vertex ui¯\bar{u_{i}} is colored red. It remains to show that this coloring is a mutual-visibility coloring.
Vertices pp and cc are in mutual-visibility with all other vertices in H2(i)H_{2}^{(i)}, for each i∈[q]i\in[q], because the color assignment satisfies that of the proof of Lemma 2.2. Clearly, vertices pp and cc are in mutual-visibility with vertex zz (z′z^{\prime}, resp.) through path p,c,u1,zp,c,u_{1},z (p,c,u1,z′p,c,u_{1},z^{\prime}, resp.) or path p,c,u1¯,zp,c,\bar{u_{1}},z (p,c,u1¯,z′p,c,\bar{u_{1}},z^{\prime}, resp.).
More interesting is the mutual-visibility of pp and cc with vertices vj,wjv_{j},w_{j}, for each fixed j∈[r]j\in[r]. These four vertices belong to H3(j)H_{3}^{(j)} and since the other three vertices in TjT_{j} cannot have the same color because tt is a satisfying truth assignment for CC, the coloring of H3(j)H_{3}^{(j)} also satisfies that of the proof of Lemma 2.2. Then pp and cc are in mutual-visibility with vertices vj,wjv_{j},w_{j}.
It remains to check the mutual-visibility of the other vertices. Vertex zz is clearly in mutual-visibility with each vertex ss in ⋃i∈[q]V⁡(H2(i))∪⋃j∈[r]V⁡(H3(j))∖{p,c}\bigcup_{i\in[q]}V(H_{2}^{(i)})\cup\bigcup_{j\in[r]}V(H_{3}^{(j)})\setminus\{p,c\}, since any shortest x,sx,s-path PP has length at most two and and when the length is two at least two vertices in PP have different colors. Similarly for z′z^{\prime}.
Any vertex xx in A={ui,ui¯|i∈[q]}A=\{u_{i},\bar{u_{i}}~|~i\in[q]\} is in mutual-visibility with any vertex yy in B={ui,ui¯,ai,bi|i∈[q]}∪{vj,wj|j∈[r]}B=\{u_{i},\bar{u_{i}},a_{i},b_{i}~|~i\in[q]\}\cup\{v_{j},w_{j}~|~j\in[r]\}, because if d⁡(x,y)=2d(x,y)=2 we can choose a shortest x,yx,y-path PP passing through either zz or z′z^{\prime} to guarantee a two coloring of PP, and if d⁡(x,y)=3d(x,y)=3, that is y=biy=b_{i} or y=wjy=w_{j}, for any i∈[q]i\in[q] or any j∈[r]j\in[r], there is a shortest x,yx,y-path passing throw either zz or z′z^{\prime} such that the first two vertices and the last two vertices are colored with different colors.
Finally, any vertex xx in {ai,bi,vj,wj|i∈[q],j∈[r]}\{a_{i},b_{i},v_{j},w_{j}~|~i\in[q],j\in[r]\} is in mutual-visibility with any other vertex yy in the same set because the subgraph HH induced by the vertices {ai,bi,z,z′,vj,wj}\{a_{i},b_{i},z,z^{\prime},v_{j},w_{j}\} is isomorphic to H2H_{2} and the distances between two vertices in HH are the same as those in GG. Since the coloring of the vertices in HH is the coloring used in Lemma 2.2, xx and yy are mutually visible.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow) Conversely, suppose that there is a mutual-visibility coloring of the graph GG with two colors. Since the subgraphs H2(i)H_{2}^{(i)}, for each i∈[q]i\in[q], and H3(j)H_{3}^{(j)}, for each j∈[r]j\in[r], of GG are isomorphic to the graphs H2H_{2} and H3H_{3}, by Lemma 2.2 all pairs of vertices p,cp,c; ui,ui¯u_{i},\bar{u_{i}} and ai,bia_{i},b_{i}, for each i∈[q]i\in[q]; vj,wjv_{j},w_{j}, for each j∈[r]j\in[r], must be colored with different colors. The pair z,z′z,z^{\prime} must also be colored with two colors by the same lemma, because the subgraph induced by vertices a1,b1,z,z′,v1,w1a_{1},b_{1},z,z^{\prime},v_{1},w_{1} is isomorphic to H2H_{2}.

Since the vertices uiu_{i} and ui¯\bar{u_{i}} of a H2(i)H_{2}^{(i)} subgraph, for each i∈[q]i\in[q], have different colors, we assign the value T​r​u​eTrue to variable xix_{i} if the vertex uiu_{i} is colored red, whereas we assign the value F​a​l​s​eFalse to variable xix_{i} if the vertices uiu_{i} is colored white. Now, by contradiction, assume that the instance Φ\Phi of NAE3-SAT is not satisfied. This means that there exists a clause ch∈Cc_{h}\in C, for a certain h∈[r]h\in[r], such that all three literals of chc_{h} have the same truth value. In turn, this implies that all the vertices in ThT_{h} have the same color, but this contradicts Lemma 2.2 applied to subgraph H3(h)H_{3}^{(h)}. In particular, there would be a vertex in x∈{p,c}x\in\{p,c\} and a vertex y∈{vh,wh}y\in\{v_{h},w_{h}\} that are not in mutual-visibility, since they would have the same color as the vertices in ThT_{h}. ∎

3 Mutual-visibility coloring in glued tt-ary trees

As the mutual-visibility coloring problem is NP-complete even for instances (G,k)(G,k) with d​i​a​m​(G)=4diam(G)=4 and k=2k=2, it is worth investigating the problem in special classes of graphs. The exact value of mutual-visibility chromatic number of the glued tt-ary trees are determined in this section. We start with the special case of the glued binary trees and then extend the result to glued tt-ary trees.

Throughout this section, the vertices of two copies of the binary tree in G​T​(r)GT(r) are denoted by vi,jv_{i,j} and vi,j′v_{i,j}^{\prime}, respectively, for i=1,2,…,r−1i=1,2,\ldots,r-1 and i−1i-1 is the depth of vi,jv_{i,j} and vi,j′v^{\prime}_{i,j} in Tr(1)T_{r}^{(1)} and Tr(2)T_{r}^{(2)}, respectively; and jj is the position of the vertex counted from left to right in the drawing. The quasi-leaves, which are leaf vertices of both rooted binary trees, are denoted by v1,v2,…​…​v2rv_{1},v_{2},......v_{2^{r}}, labeled from left to right in the drawing. See Figure 3 for the denotation of the vertices in graph G​T​(3)GT(3) and graph G​T​(4)GT(4).

Let viv_{i} and vjv_{j} be two quasi-leaves of G​T​(r)GT(r). There exist exactly two geodesic paths between viv_{i} and vjv_{j}, say Pi,jP_{i,j}, through Vr(1)V_{r}^{(1)} and Pi,j′P^{\prime}_{i,j} through Vr(2)V_{r}^{(2)}. Now, Pi,jP_{i,j} and Pi,j′P^{\prime}_{i,j} together induces a cycle which we denote by Ci,jC_{i,j}. Let Qi,jQ_{i,j} and Qi,j′Q_{i,j}^{\prime} be the paths Pi,j\{vi,vj}P_{i,j}\backslash\{v_{i},v_{j}\} and paths Pi,j′\{vi,vj}P_{i,j}^{\prime}\backslash\{v_{i},v_{j}\}, respectively. Note that any cycle in G​T​(r)GT(r) intersects with exactly two quasi-leaves and can always be represented as Ci,jC_{i,j} in a unique manner.

The following observations related to the geodesic paths between any two vertices in G​T​(r)GT(r) will be useful for us.

Observation 3.1.

Given two vertices of the form vi,jv_{i,j} and vk,lv_{k,l} in a copy of a binary tree, there exists a unique geodesic path between them.

Observation 3.2.

Given two vertices vi,j∈Tr(1)v_{i,j}\in T^{(1)}_{r}, vi,j′∈Tr(2)v^{\prime}_{i,j}\in T^{(2)}_{r} and any leaf vertex vav_{a} of Tvi,jT_{v_{i,j}} (equivalently, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁Tvi,j′)T_{v^{\prime}_{i,j}}), then there exists a unique geodesic path between vi,jv_{i,j} and vi,j′v^{\prime}_{i,j}, which passes through vav_{a}.

Observation 3.3.

Given two vertices vi,j∈Tr(1)v_{i,j}\in T^{(1)}_{r}, vi,l′∈Tr(2)v^{\prime}_{i,l}\in T^{(2)}_{r} and any leaf vertex vav_{a} of Tvi,jT_{v_{i,j}} (equivalently, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁Tvi,l′)T_{v^{\prime}_{i,l}}), then there exists a unique geodesic path between vi,jv_{i,j} and vi,l′v^{\prime}_{i,l}, which passes through vav_{a}. Also each of these geodesic paths, either passes through vi,j′v^{\prime}_{i,j} or vi,lv_{i,l}.

Observation 3.4.

Given two vertices vi,j∈Tr(1)v_{i,j}\in T^{(1)}_{r}, vk,l′∈Tr(2)v^{\prime}_{k,l}\in T^{(2)}_{r} where i<ki<k and any leaf vertex vav_{a} of Tvk,lT_{v_{k,l}}, then there exists a unique geodesic path between vi,jv_{i,j} and vk,l′v^{\prime}_{k,l}, which passes through vav_{a} and each of these geodesic paths passes through vk,lv_{k,l} also. Also, a similar statement holds for k<ik<i.

Lemma 3.5.

If SS is a mutual-visibility set of G​T​(r)GT(r), then |S∩V⁡(Ci,j)|≤3|{S\cap V(C_{i,j})}|\leq 3.

Proof.

Assume the contrary that there exists a mutual-visibility set SS of G​T​(r)GT(r) such that |S∩V⁡(Ci,j)|>3|S\cap V(C_{i,j})|>3.

If both quasi-leaves in Ci,jC_{i,j} are present in SS, then |S∩V⁡(Qi,j)|≤1|S\cap V(Q_{i,j})|\leq 1 and |S∩V⁡(Qi,j′)|≤1|S\cap V(Q_{i,j}^{\prime})|\leq 1. Also, SS cannot simultaneously intersect V⁡(Qi,j)V(Q_{i,j}) and V⁡(Qi,j′)V(Q_{i,j}^{\prime}) and hence |S∩V⁡(Ci,j)|≤3|S\cap V(C_{i,j})|\leq 3. If one of the quasi-leaves in Ci,jC_{i,j} is present in SS, then again |S∩V⁡(Qi,j)|≤1|S\cap V(Q_{i,j})|\leq 1 and |S∩V⁡(Qi,j′)|≤1|S\cap V(Q_{i,j}^{\prime})|\leq 1, and hence |S∩V⁡(Ci,j)|≤3|{S\cap V(C_{i,j})}|\leq 3.

Now consider the case where both the quasi-leaves are not present in SS. Since the quasi-leaves are not present in SS, then since |S∩V⁡(Qi,j)|≤2|S\cap V(Q_{i,j})|\leq 2 and |S∩V⁡(Qi,j′)|≤2|S\cap V(Q_{i,j}^{\prime})|\leq 2, we have |S∩V⁡(Ci,j)|≤4|{S\cap V(C_{i,j})}|\leq 4. But, if there are two vertices each from both Qi,jQ_{i,j} and Qi,j′Q^{\prime}_{i,j}, say vi,j,vk,l,va,b′v_{i,j},v_{k,l},v^{\prime}_{a,b} and vc,d′v^{\prime}_{c,d}, then from the above observations, at least one pair of these vertices will not be mutually-visible, which is a contradiction. Hence, the lemma. ∎

The general position variation of mutual-visibility chromatic number was introduced by [4] in 2024. The minimum number of colors required to color the vertices of GG such that each color class is in general position is called general position chromatic number, denoted by χgp​(G)\chi_{\text{gp}}(G). The color classes obtained in the proof of Theorem 3.6 are also in general position except for r=2i−1+2i−2+i−2r=2^{i-1}+2^{i-2}+i-2. Hence, we have the following corollary.

Corollary 3.7.

If r≥2r\geq 2 and r≠2i−1+2i−2+i−2r\neq 2^{i-1}+2^{i-2}+i-2 then χg​p​(G​T​(r))=χμ​(G​T​(r))\chi_{gp}(GT(r))=\chi_{\mu}(GT(r)).

But then cc will be used at least four times in one of the cycles Cm​tr−n,p​tr−qC_{mt^{r-n},pt^{r-q}}, C(m+1)​tr−n,p​tr−qC_{(m+1)t^{r-n},pt^{r-q}}, Cm​tr−n,(p+1)​tr−qC_{mt^{r-n},(p+1)t^{r-q}} and C(m+1)​tr−n,(p+1)​tr−qC_{(m+1)t^{r-n},(p+1)t^{r-q}}, which contradicts Lemma 3.8. Therefore, χmn∩χpq=ϕ\chi^{n}_{m}\cap\chi^{q}_{p}=\phi.

Note that we have considered 1+(t−1)+t⁡(t−1)+t2​(t−1)+…+ti−2​(t−1)=1+ti−1−1=ti−11+(t-1)+t(t-1)+t^{2}(t-1)+\ldots+t^{i-2}(t-1)=1+t^{i-1}-1=t^{i-1} cycles. Since all the tn−1t^{n}-1 cycles χmn\chi^{n}_{m} are disjoint and since cardinality of elements in χmn\chi^{n}_{m} is at least 4​i−4​n−24i-4n-2, if m≢1(modt)m\not\equiv 1\pmod{t} and 4​i−4​n−44i-4n-4, if m≡1(modt)m\equiv 1\pmod{t} implies that |⋃m,nχmn|≥∑n=1i−1((t−2)​tn−1​(4​i−4​n−2)+tn−1​(4​i−4​n−4))=2​(ti−1)t−1|\bigcup_{m,n}\chi^{n}_{m}|\geq\sum_{n=1}^{i-1}\Bigl((t-2)t^{n-1}(4i-4n-2)+t^{n-1}(4i-4n-4)\Bigr)=\frac{2(t^{i}-1)}{t-1}. Therefore, at least 2​(ti−1)t−1\frac{2(t^{i}-1)}{t-1} colors are used three times to color G​T​(r,t)GT(r,t). But, we have only 2​(r−i)+12(r-i)+1 colors and r≤ti−1t−1+i−1r\leq\frac{t^{i}-1}{t-1}+i-1 so that 2​(r−i)+1≤2​(ti−1)t−1−12(r-i)+1\leq\frac{2(t^{i}-1)}{t-1}-1, a contradiction.
Therefore, at least 2​(r−i)+22(r-i)+2 colors are required for a mutual-visibility coloring of G​T​(r,t)GT(r,t). Now, let us investigate whether 2​(r−i)+22(r-i)+2 colors are sufficient. Suppose we have 2​(r−i)+22(r-i)+2 colors. Consider the cycles CmnC_{m}^{n}, n∈[i−2]n\in[i-2]. Then by similar arguments, all these cycles are disjoint and cardinality of elements in χmn\chi^{n}_{m} is at least 4​i−4​n−44i-4n-4, if m≢1(modt)m\not\equiv 1\pmod{t} and 4​i−4​n−64i-4n-6, if m≡1(modt)m\equiv 1\pmod{t}, implies that |⋃n,mχnm|≥2​(ti−1−1)t−1+2​ti−2|\bigcup_{n,m}\chi^{m}_{n}|\geq\frac{2(t^{i-1}-1)}{t-1}+2t^{i-2}, n∈[i−2]n\in[i-2]. Let SS be the collection of all vertices of depth (i−1)(i-1) of Tr(1)T_{r}^{(1)} that are not part of any CmnC_{m}^{n} for n∈[i−2]n\in[i-2]. Note that |S|=ti−1−2​ti−2|S|=t^{i-1}-2t^{i-2} and |S|>0|S|>0 for t≥3t\geq 3. Let TT be the collection of quasi-leaves obtained by taking one quasi-leaf of the binary tree rooted at kk, for each k∈Sk\in S. Now consider the cycles Ck,lC_{k,l} where k,l∈Tk,l\in T. In each of these cycles there are exactly 2​(r−i+3)2(r-i+3) vertices that are not part of any CmnC_{m}^{n}, n∈[i−2]n\in[i-2]. Since we have only 2​(r−i)+22(r-i)+2 colors, at least two colors must be repeated at least three times in every cycle, and these colors are distinct. Using similar arguments, we can prove that these colors are also distinct from χmn\chi_{m}^{n}, n∈[i−2]n\in[i-2]. Therefore, at least 2​(ti−1−1)t−1−2​ti−2+ti−1−2​ti−2=2​(ti−1−1)t−1+ti−1\frac{2(t^{i-1}-1)}{t-1}-2t^{i-2}+t^{i-1}-2t^{i-2}=\frac{2(t^{i-1}-1)}{t-1}+t^{i-1} distinct colors must be used to color G​T​(r,t)GT(r,t). But in this case, if r≤ti−1−1t−1+ti−12+i−2r\leq\frac{t^{i-1}-1}{t-1}+\frac{t^{i-1}}{2}+i-2, so that 2​(r−i)+2≤2​(ti−1−1)t−1+ti−1−22(r-i)+2\leq\frac{2(t^{i-1}-1)}{t-1}+t^{i-1}-2. Hence, the theorem. ∎

4 Concluding Remarks

In this paper we prove the NP-completeness of the mutual-visibility coloring problem, which was left as an open question in [14], reinforcing the theoretical challenge in determining the mutual-visibility chromatic number of arbitrary graphs and providing strong motivation to find the exact value and tight bounds for specific graph classes. We also determine the exact value of glued binary trees and glued tt-ary trees. Several natural directions remains open for future investigation. In particular finding the mutual-visibility chromatic number of highly symmetric or self similar structures such as the hypercubes, hypercube-like graphs, the Hamming graphs and the generalized Sierpiński graphs, including Sierpiński triangle graphs and Sierpiński gasket graphs are interesting.
